# 1.5 Example 4

## Step 1 – Recognizing an Argument

Let's consider the following passage, asking ourselves **"What is this
passage doing? Is it trying to convince us that something is true?"**

> "Are you wondering which brand of soap is the superior product? This
> magazine ad shows someone giving a very good presentation at work
> after using Cool and Fresh soap, so Cool and Fresh soap must be the
> best."

I think that this passage does contain an argument because it's trying
to establish that one claim is true by citing other claims as evidence.
There's an inference indicator in this passage as well, the little word
"so," which can help us to see that reasons are being given to support a
claim.

> "Are you wondering which brand of soap is the superior product? This
> magazine ad shows someone giving a very good presentation at work
> after using Cool and Fresh soap, **so** Cool and Fresh soap must be
> the best."

## Step 2 – Analyzing the Argument

We'll start to analyze this argument by identifying the ultimate
conclusion, asking ourselves, **"What is the ultimate conclusion, or the
main claim that this argument is trying to get us to believe?"**

Because inference indicator expressions can help us out here, let's
focus on the "so." To determine whether "so" is a conclusion indicator
expression or a reason indicator expression, let's replace the "so" with
"therefore," then replace the "so" with "because," and see which passage
is more like the original.

In this case, we get

> "Are you wondering which brand of soap is the superior product? This
> magazine ad shows someone giving a very good presentation at work
> after using Cool and Fresh soap, **therefore** Cool and Fresh soap
> must be the best."

and

> "Are you wondering which brand of soap is the superior product? This
> magazine ad shows someone giving a very good presentation at work
> after using Cool and Fresh soap, **because** Cool and Fresh soap must
> be the best."

Since it seems as though the first passage is more similar to the
original, "so" works like "therefore" and not like "because." It's a
conclusion indicator expression, not a reason indicator expression.

(By the way, this is a nice way to determine whether an inference
indicator expression is a conclusion indicator expression or a reason
indicator expression. First replace the expression with "therefore";
then replace it with "because," and see which passage is more like the
original. Of course, you can look at the list of inference expressions,
too, but sometimes you won't have that list handy and some inference
indicator expressions aren't on the list, so it's a good idea to have a
way to figure this out for yourself when you need to.)

Because "so" is a conclusion indicator expression, we know that "Cool
and Fresh soap must be the best" is the conclusion of this argument.

> "Are you wondering which brand of soap is the superior product? This
> magazine ad shows someone giving a very good presentation at work
> after using Cool and Fresh soap, **so** (1) Cool and Fresh soap must
> be the best."

Returning to the beginning of the passage, our next questions are,
**"What else is being claimed?"** and **"Is this claim part of the
argument?"** With this in mind, what should we do with the first
sentence, "Are you wondering which brand of soap is the superior
product?"

That sentence is the first question that we've encountered in a passage
that contains an argument. Is it part of the argument itself?

Well, arguments are composed of claims. Claims are either true or false
(even if we're not sure which it is), so a test for determining whether
or not a sentence expresses a claim is to see whether or not it makes
any sense for us to agree or disagree with it.

When we apply that test, we see that **questions usually don't convey
claims because they usually can't be true or false.** If I asked you
"Are you wondering which brand of soap is the superior product?" you
could answer "No. I'm not wondering which brand of soap is the superior
product," but you couldn't really sensibly say "False! That question is
false!" Normally, then, questions don't convey claims at all and so
won't be included in our list of important claims. Let's just ignore the
first sentence of this passage.

(Will we always be ignoring questions? No. In a subsequent chapter,
we'll see special kinds of questions that *do* in fact convey claims,
but for now we'll be ignoring questions because *normal* questions can't
be true or false and because in this chapter we'll only be dealing with
normal questions like that.)

Finally, what should we do with the sentence "This magazine ad shows
someone giving a very good presentation at work after using Cool and
Fresh soap"? Does that convey a claim that's part of the argument?

I think so. For one thing, if we don't include it, we'll have only one
claim -- the ultimate conclusion. And if we only have one claim -- the
ultimate conclusion -- we won't have any support for the ultimate
conclusion and so won't have an argument. For another thing, this claim
is connected to our ultimate conclusion with a "so," which indicates
that there will be an inference going from one of these claims to the
other. We definitely want to include this claim in the argument.

> "Are you wondering which brand of soap is the superior product? (2)
> This magazine ad shows someone giving a very good presentation at work
> after using Cool and Fresh soap, **so** (1) Cool and Fresh soap must
> be the best."

With these claims identified, we can ask ourselves, **"How are these
claims connected to each other?"** And, as will often be the case, the
inference indicator expression tells us. Because "so" is a conclusion
indicator expression, we know that claim 1 follows from claim 2. That
gives us the following argument map:

> "Are you wondering which brand of soap is the superior product? (2)
> This magazine ad shows someone giving a very good presentation at work
> after using Cool and Fresh soap, **so** (1) Cool and Fresh soap must
> be the best."

![Map of the soap advertisement argument.](/images/ch01/Advertisement4.png){#fig-1-5-ad-1 width=313px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) Cool and Fresh soap must be the best. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-5-ad-1"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement4_list.md >}}
:::

## Step 3 – Evaluating the Argument

We've learned to evaluate premises by asking ourselves **"Is this
premise true?"** and **"Could someone who doesn't already believe the
ultimate conclusion believe this premise?"** so let's do that here.

Our premise is "This magazine ad shows someone giving a very good
presentation at work after using Cool and Fresh soap." Is that true? Of
course we're not looking at the magazine ad right now, but let's take
for granted that the premise is true.

Now, could someone who doesn't already believe the conclusion, "Cool and
Fresh soap must be the best," believe the premise? I think so. This
means that we've finally seen an argument with a good premise!

> "Are you wondering which brand of soap is the superior product? (2)
> This magazine ad shows someone giving a very good presentation at work
> after using Cool and Fresh soap, **so** (1) Cool and Fresh soap must
> be the best."

![Map of the soap advertisement argument, with the premise evaluated as good.](/images/ch01/Advertisement4_P_Eval.png){#fig-1-5-ad-p-eval-1 width=313px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) Cool and Fresh soap must be the best. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-5-ad-p-eval-1"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement4_P_Eval_list.md >}}
:::

But is this a *good argument?* Does it, in other words, establish that
its conclusion is probably true? I don't think so. **The problem with
this argument lies with the inference**.

An inference, remember, is the connection that holds between two claims
when the truth of one of them (in this case, claim 2) is supposed to
establish the truth of the other (in this case, claim 1).

But claim 2 in this argument *doesn't* establish the truth of claim 1.
The fact that a magazine ad shows someone giving a very good
presentation at work after using Cool and Fresh soap (claim 2) doesn't
establish that Cool and Fresh soap is the best (claim 1) because a
photograph and some dialogue doesn't establish that there's any causal
relationship between Cool and Fresh soap and strong performance on the
job. (And, even if there *were* such a relationship, it wouldn't be
enough to prove that Cool and Fresh soap is the best since many other
soaps might have the same result, since Cool and Fresh soap could have
nasty side effects, and so on.) In short, *the connection between the
premise and conclusion here isn't very strong*. The inference in this
argument is pretty bad.

Remember how we call an objection that asserts that a premise is false a
"'not so' objection" because it looks at that premise and says, in
effect, "That's not so"? We'll call an objection that asserts that an
inference is weak a "'so what' objection" because it looks at a claim
and says, in effect, "So what? Even if this is true, we can't safely
arrive at the conclusion from here because the bridge is so bad."

We can note in the map that the inference is bad.

> "Are you wondering which brand of soap is the superior product? (2)
> This magazine ad shows someone giving a very good presentation at work
> after using Cool and Fresh soap, **so** (1) Cool and Fresh soap must
> be the best."

![Map of the soap advertisement argument, with the premise evaluated as good and the inference evaluated as bad.](/images/ch01/Advertisement4_I_Eval.png){#fig-1-5-ad-i-eval-1 width=313px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) Cool and Fresh soap must be the best. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-5-ad-i-eval-1"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement4_I_Eval_list.md >}}
:::

And because this bad inference prevents the argument from establishing
the ultimate conclusion, this argument is bad.

> "Are you wondering which brand of soap is the superior product? (2)
> This magazine ad shows someone giving a very good presentation at work
> after using Cool and Fresh soap, **so** (1) Cool and Fresh soap must
> be the best."

![Map of the soap advertisement argument, with the premise evaluated as good and the inference evaluated as bad.](/images/ch01/Advertisement4_I_Eval.png){#fig-1-5-ad-i-eval-2 width=313px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) Cool and Fresh soap must be the best. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-5-ad-i-eval-2"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement4_I_Eval_list.md >}}
:::

Note: This argument is bad because it has a bad inference.

### Evaluating Inferences and the Map Analogy

As we've seen, it's often helpful to think of an argument like an
attempt to direct us to a big, golden, boulder. The premise is the
boulder that we start from. The ultimate conclusion is our destination.
And the inference is the bridge that connects the two.

![](/images/ch01/ladder_good.png){.illustration width=141px fig-alt="A sturdy wooden ladder leads from a gray boulder up to a golden boulder."}

Examples 1 and 2 showed us that if we can't stand on our starting
boulder (because the premise is false or assumes the conclusion), the
argument won't help us reach the golden boulder.

![](/images/ch01/ladder_cracked_boulder.png){.illustration width=121px fig-alt="A wooden ladder leads up to a golden boulder, but the gray boulder it stands on is split by a crack."}

Now we've learned that we might not be able to reach the golden boulder
because the bridge breaks down. Accordingly, if the inference is weak
then the argument is bad too.

![](/images/ch01/ladder_broken.png){.illustration width=172px fig-alt="A wooden ladder rises from a gray boulder toward a golden boulder, but the ladder is snapped in two in the middle."}

Just like a dependable path needs to give us boulders we can stand on
and bridges that are strong, a good argument needs good premises and
good inferences. And just as boulders and bridges are not the same,
**premises and inferences are very different things**.

### The "Gully Test" for Evaluating Inferences

Because premises and inferences are such different things, and because
it's *very* easy to confuse our evaluation of a premise with our
evaluation of an inference, we'll evaluate inferences with the
"Perfectly Gullible but Perfectly Rational Person (Gully) Test." To use
this test, we ask ourselves, **"If a perfectly gullible, perfectly
rational person (we could call him 'Gully' for short) believes the
reasons, how likely is that person to believe the conclusion?"** If
Gully is highly likely to believe the conclusion on the basis of the
reasons, then the inference is good. If Gully is not likely to believe
the conclusion on the basis of the reasons, then the inference is bad.

It's easy to see how this test would indicate that the inference in the
argument that we're looking at is bad. If we tell Gully, "The magazine
ad shows someone giving a presentation at work after using Cool and
Fresh soap," Gully would not, on the basis of that, be inclined to think
that Cool and Fresh soap must be the best. Gully is rational, after all,
so he'd have all the concerns about the inference that we do.

The Gully Test can really help us out -- but please remember that the
Gully Test is used to evaluate inferences and *not* to evaluate
premises! Since Gully believes everything we tell him and since we'll be
telling him to believe all of the premises, Gully will like *all*
premises, no matter how outlandish! We just can't depend upon Gully to
help us decide whether or not a premise is good; he's far too gullible
for that. According to Gully, *all* premises are good.

### Communicating Our Evaluation

Although our evaluation of an inference should be unaffected by our
assessment of the reasons from which the inference stems, the way in
which we *communicate* that assessment will often be a function of our
attitude toward that reason.

If we happen to like the reason in an inference but think that the
inference is bad, we can use the **"just because... it doesn't follow
that..."** construction, saying "Just because \[state the reason here\],
it doesn't follow that \[state the conclusion here\] because \[explain
how the reason can be true and the conclusion false at the same time\]."

In the case of the argument we've evaluated, for instance, we can say,
"Just because this magazine ad shows someone giving a very good
presentation at work after using Cool and Fresh soap, it doesn't follow
that Cool and Fresh soap must be the best because a photograph and some
dialogue doesn't establish that there's any causal relationship between
Cool and Fresh soap and strong performance on the job."

Of course, if we *don't* happen to like the reason in an inference then
we *won't* want to use the "Just because... it doesn't follow that..."
construction, because that will sound like we endorse the reason. We
will, instead, want to use the **"Even if... it wouldn't follow
that..."** construction, saying "Even if \[state the reason here\], it
wouldn't follow that \[state the conclusion here\] because \[explain how
the reason can be true and the conclusion false at the same time\]."

For example, suppose we discover that the magazine ad was *not* for Cool
and Fresh soap but was, instead, for Rise and Shine energy supplement.
In that case, we would say, "Even if this magazine ad showed someone
giving a very good presentation at work after using Cool and Fresh soap
(which, of course, it doesn't because the ad is for an energy
supplement), it wouldn't follow that Cool and Fresh soap must be the
best because a photograph and some dialogue doesn't establish that
there's any causal relationship between Cool and Fresh soap and strong
performance on the job."

## Summary of Example 4

The passage we considered in this example was:

> "Are you wondering which brand of soap is the superior product? This
> magazine ad shows someone giving a very good presentation at work
> after using Cool and Fresh soap, so Cool and Fresh soap must be the
> best."

### Step 1 – Recognizing an Argument

We asked, **"What is this passage doing? Is it trying to convince us
that something is true?"**

We decided that this passage is trying to convince us of something and
so does contain an argument. The inference indicator expression "so"
helped us, too.

> "Are you wondering which brand of soap is the superior product? This
> magazine ad shows someone giving a very good presentation at work
> after using Cool and Fresh soap, **so** Cool and Fresh soap must be
> the best."

### Step 2 – Analyzing the Argument

We began our analysis of the argument by asking, **"What is the ultimate
conclusion, or the main claim that this argument is trying to get us to
believe?"**

The fact that "so" is a conclusion indicator expression points to "Cool
and Fresh soap must be the best" as the ultimate conclusion.

> "Are you wondering which brand of soap is the superior product? This
> magazine ad shows someone giving a very good presentation at work
> after using Cool and Fresh soap, **so** (1) Cool and Fresh soap must
> be the best."

At this point, we returned to the beginning of the passage and asked,
**"What else is being claimed?"** and **"Is this claim part of the
argument?"**

Because the first sentence is a question and because questions don't
usually convey claims, it's not part of the argument. We ignored it.

"This magazine ad shows someone giving a very good presentation at work
after using Cool and Fresh soap," on the other hand, is part of the
argument.

> "Are you wondering which brand of soap is the superior product? (2)
> This magazine ad shows someone giving a very good presentation at work
> after using Cool and Fresh soap, **so** (1) Cool and Fresh soap must
> be the best."

At this point, we asked, **"How are these claims connected to each
other?"** "So" has already allowed us to see that claim 1 is a
conclusion following from claim 2, so we mapped the argument like this:

> "Are you wondering which brand of soap is the superior product? (2)
> This magazine ad shows someone giving a very good presentation at work
> after using Cool and Fresh soap, **so** (1) Cool and Fresh soap must
> be the best."

![Map of the soap advertisement argument.](/images/ch01/Advertisement4.png){#fig-1-5-ad-2 width=313px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) Cool and Fresh soap must be the best. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-5-ad-2"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement4_list.md >}}
:::

### Step 3 – Evaluating the Argument

We evaluated the premise by asking **"Is this premise true?"** and
**"Could someone who doesn't already believe the ultimate conclusion
believe this premise?"** Because the answer to both of these questions
was "yes," we decided that the premise is good.

> "Are you wondering which brand of soap is the superior product? (2)
> This magazine ad shows someone giving a very good presentation at work
> after using Cool and Fresh soap, **so** (1) Cool and Fresh soap must
> be the best."

![Map of the soap advertisement argument, with the premise evaluated as good.](/images/ch01/Advertisement4_P_Eval.png){#fig-1-5-ad-p-eval-2 width=313px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) Cool and Fresh soap must be the best. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-5-ad-p-eval-2"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement4_P_Eval_list.md >}}
:::

Unfortunately, the inference between the premise and the conclusion is
weak. We saw this by asking, **"If a perfectly gullible, perfectly
rational person (we could call him 'Gully' for short) believes the
premise, how likely is that person to believe the conclusion?"** Gully
could easily believe claim 2 without accepting claim 1, so inference A
is bad. That's enough to make the argument bad as a whole.

> "Are you wondering which brand of soap is the superior product? (2)
> This magazine ad shows someone giving a very good presentation at work
> after using Cool and Fresh soap, **so** (1) Cool and Fresh soap must
> be the best."

![Map of the soap advertisement argument, with the premise evaluated as good and the inference evaluated as bad.](/images/ch01/Advertisement4_I_Eval.png){#fig-1-5-ad-i-eval-3 width=313px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) Cool and Fresh soap must be the best. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-5-ad-i-eval-3"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement4_I_Eval_list.md >}}
:::

Note: This argument is bad because it has a bad inference.

An objection to an argument that asserts that an inference is weak is a
"'so what' objection" because it looks at a premise and says, in effect,
"So what?"

Although our assessment of an inference shouldn't be affected by our
assessment of the premise, the way that we *express* our criticism of an
inference *will* be influenced by our attitude toward the premise.

-   If we happen to like the reason in an inference but think that the
    inference is bad, we can use the "just because... it doesn't follow
    that..." construction, saying "Just because \[state the reason
    here\], it doesn't follow that \[state the conclusion here\] because
    \[explain how the reason can be true and the conclusion false at the
    same time\]."

-   If we don't happen to like the reason in an inference but think that
    the inference is bad, we can use the "Even if... it wouldn't follow
    that..." construction, saying "Even if \[state the reason here\], it
    wouldn't follow that \[state the conclusion here\] because \[explain
    how the reason can be true and the conclusion false at the same
    time\]."
